To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the volatility of the DJIA components is less asymmetric than that implied by the index itself and that this asymmetry is more pronounced with regard to index news than firm-specific news.
the volatility of the 30 Dow Jones Industrial Average stocks responds more asymmetrically with respect to past market returns than to past firm-specific returns.

individual stock volatility processes are more responsive to lagged signed index returns than to lagged signed firm-specific returns, and this asymmetry is more pronounced for the index than for individual stock returns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of firm-specific returns and of signed index returns on the conditional variances of individual stocks.
the volatility processes of 30 individual stocks and their relationship with the volatility of the parent index over a ten year period.
the impact of market news on the volatility processes and on the asymmetric response of individual stocks’ volatility to past news.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the volatility of individual stocks responds asymmetrically to market news, and to a much lesser extent to firm-specific news.
individual stock returns are asymmetrically related to both firm specific and index returns.
individual stocks’ volatility responds more asymmetricly to signed index returns than to signed firm-specific returns.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the volatility of individual stocks is more responsive to the news conveyed in market returns than in firm-specific returns, and that the volatility of the DJIA itself is asymmetric with respect to market returns.
the asymmetric volatility process of a stock is more closely associated with the market’s volatility than with its own firm specific information.
individual stock volatility processes are more asymmetric than that of their parent index, but they are more correlated with market returns than with firm-specific returns.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the volatility asymmetry is a market-wide effect, which is not necessarily related to the leverage effect or volatility feedback.
individual stock volatility processes are more sensitive to market returns than firm-specific returns.
individual stock volatility processes respond to market news more than they respond to firm specific news.
